history.excerpt:
The cup sounds expensive when you slow it down. Its base catches on the table, a short ceramic complaint, and through the headphones it becomes something much larger moving reluctantly.

Úna Carroll leans towards the playback at the introductory theatre-sound session. “Keep that. Might be useful for the door.”

There is already a door in the rehearsal room. You look at it.

“Not that door,” she says. “The one we haven't got.”

You try the scrape again. This time you press too hard and the cup tips. Úna catches it, laughing, then goes back to working out an entrance. Nobody asks whether you have found your calling. By the end of the session, you have agreed to help with the rehearsal run and a matinee. It is something you can actually try alongside the administration job, rather than another field to read about after work.

At home, Tunde stands beside the table with his dinner while you listen to another take.

“Can I have this bit?” He indicates the place occupied by your elbow, the cup and a trailing cable.

You lift the equipment onto your lap. He sits down, and the scrape of his chair enters the recording. You both hear it on playback. Tunde laughs with his mouth full. You save

chapter.title: The Breath on the Page
chapter.body:
Úna crosses the rehearsal room and you click the latch after she has already turned.

“Again,” she says, returning to the far wall.

You check the small piece of metal in your hand. It works. You have been watching it work.

This time you look at her shoulder. There is a slight lift before she turns, enough warning to move your thumb. The click arrives with her movement. She crosses back without commenting, and you write down what you saw.

By the end of that July evening, the margin has become more useful than the printed lines. Arrows point towards other arrows. You have written ‘not yet’ beside a place where you kept coming in early.

“Would I know what that means?” Úna asks.

“You'd know if you'd been here.”

“Yes, but that's the difficulty.”

She needs the notes to outlast the person holding them. You add an explanation beneath ‘not yet’, then draw a box around both. It is beginning to resemble something you might produce at the administration job, except that a perfectly orderly page can still send you wrong.

The remaining sessions fit into evenings after work. You eat before leaving, arrive with your head full, and spend the first few minutes trying to hear the room instead. By September, the sequence no longer feels like a succession of emergencies. Your hand can find the latch without your eyes helping it.

During the final run, you hold it ready for so long that the edge presses a pale groove into your finger. You resist shifting your grip. The cue comes; you make the sound; the scene continues. Nobody looks over. That absence of attention gives you a small, unexpected pleasure.

Afterwards, Úna asks what you thought of the changed exchange near the end.

“The pause?” you say.

“No, before that.”

You cannot place it. You remember waiting for the next effect, then checking the mark beneath your thumb on the page. She describes the exchange, expecting recognition, and you have to tell her you missed it.

“But I got the sequence through.”

“You did.” She sounds tired, not disappointed. “That's the sessions done, then.”

You leave with a usable cue sheet and an oddly incomplete account of the play you have just helped perform.

In November, her message puts a fee against the familiar work: €240 for three Saturday performances in February and March, with preparation and a rehearsal included. The performances are local. The job is to operate the existing effects.

You read the amount again. Someone has allowed money for a thing you know how to do.

When Clodagh visits, you show her the message before she has taken off her coat.

“Paid sound work,” you say.

“Oh, look at you.” She smiles, and you feel yourself smiling back harder than you intended.

You fetch the cue sheet. She follows your finger from the printed line to the arrow, then to the boxed instruction beneath it.

“That's all for one noise?”

“The noise is the easy bit.”

She hands the page back carefully. “I'm going for a walk before it gets dark. Are you coming?”

You put the sheet inside its folder. Outside, the pavement is wet and you have to lengthen your stride to catch her. You reach the corner without having checked the message again.

The administration job continues. The offer stays unanswered.

At a January rehearsal, you sit where you can see the whole playing space while Úna uses your notes. There is a particular pleasure in having empty hands. Then she reaches the annotation about a breath.

She looks at the page, looks up, and misses it.

You feel the timing in your own chest: the intake, the held fraction, the place where your thumb would move. Her click comes later. It still gives the scene somewhere to go.

During the break, she brings the sheet over.

“Which breath?”

You point to the mark. “Just before the turn.”

“I can't hear that from there.”

“No. I can see it.”

“Well, I can't see it either.” She isn't smiling. She has been trying to follow the instructions you left her.

You demonstrate, lifting your shoulder slightly. She tries it, more exaggerated than you meant, and you both laugh. But when she asks whether her later cue was wrong, you cannot honestly say it was.

“I still like it earlier,” you tell her.

“All right.” She keeps hold of the sheet. “I need to get back to the cast.”

You stand to let her past. “I haven't decided about the performances.”

“I know,” she says. “I haven't booked you.”

You remember waiting for the next effect, then checking the mark beneath your thumb on the page. She describes the exchange, expecting recognition, and you have to tell her you missed it."},{"index":16,"text":"“But I got the sequence through.”"},{"index":17,"text":"“You did.” She sounds tired, not disappointed. “That's the sessions done, then.”"},{"index":18,"text":"You leave with a usable cue sheet and an oddly incomplete account of the play you have just helped perform."},{"index":19,"text":"In November, her message puts a fee against the familiar work: €240 for three Saturday performances in February and March, with preparation and a rehearsal included. The performances are local. The job is to operate the existing effects."},{"index":20,"text":"You read the amount again. Someone has allowed money for a thing you know how to do."},{"index":21,"text":"When Clodagh visits, you show her the message before she has taken off her coat."},{"index":22,"text":"“Paid sound work,” you say."},{"index":23,"text":"“Oh, look at you.” She smiles, and you feel yourself smiling back harder than you intended."},{"index":24,"text":"You fetch the cue sheet. She follows your finger from the printed line to the arrow, then to the boxed instruction beneath it."},{"index":25,"text":"“That's all for one noise?”"},{"index":26,"text":"“The noise is the easy bit.”"},{"index":27,"text":"She hands the page back carefully. “I'm going for a walk before it gets dark. Are you coming?”"},{"index":28,"text":"You put the sheet inside its folder. Outside, the pavement is wet and you have to lengthen your stride to catch her. You reach the corner without having checked the message again."},{"index":29,"text":"The administration job continues. The offer stays unanswered."},{"index":30,"text":"At a January rehearsal, you sit where you can see the whole playing space while Úna uses your notes. There is a particular pleasure in having empty hands. Then she reaches the annotation about a breath."},{"index":31,"text":"She looks at the page, looks up, and misses it."},{"index":32,"text":"You feel the timing in your own chest: the intake, the held fraction, the place where your thumb would move. Her click comes later. It still gives the scene somewhere to go."},{"index":33,"text":"During the break, she brings the sheet over."},{"index":34,"text":"“Which breath?”"},{"index":35,"text":"You point to the mark. “Just before the turn.”"},{"index":36,"text":"“I can't hear that from there.”"},{"index":37,"text":"“No. I can see it.”"},{"index":38,"text":"“Well, I can't see it either.” She isn't smiling. She has been trying to follow the instructions you left her."},{"index":39,"text":"You demonstrate, lifting your shoulder slightly. She tries it, more exaggerated than you meant, and you both laugh. But when she asks whether her later cue was wrong, you cannot honestly say it was."},{"index":40,"text":"“I still like it earlier,” you tell her."},{"index":41,"text":"“All right.” She keeps hold of the sheet. “I need to get back to the cast.”"},{"index":42,"text":"You stand to let her past. “I haven't decided about the performances.”"},{"index":43,"text":"“I know,” she says. “I haven't booked you.”"}]}
